_comment: THE T-80 HULL — running gear and lower hull only. No turret, no gun: this is the base
everything else bolts onto, and it is deliberately finished before anything is added,
because a turret is the easiest thing in the world to look at and the tracks are where
every previous silhouette correction on this project actually came from.
Authored from reference photographs at incoming/factions/russian-federation/units/t80/
(gitignored: third-party rights, and they inform PARAMETERS only — proportion, spacing,
palette — never pixels).
+X is FORWARD, +Y is LEFT, Z is up, z = 0 is the ground. A part's `at` is the CENTRE of
its box, so a wheel of radius 2.6 sitting on the belt has `at` z = 3.4.
WHAT THE REFERENCE ACTUALLY SAYS, in the order it changes the model:
1. SIX BIG ROAD WHEELS, WITH REAL GAPS. Each is about a third of a diameter clear of
the next — not the sliver the T-80's reputation for close-packed running gear
suggests. This is the tank's identity from the side and the reason the wheels are
GEOMETRY here rather than paint. They are also PAINTED OLIVE, lighter than the hull;
the dark thing down there is the TRACK.
2. THE TRACK IS ALMOST A RECTANGLE. 87% of the belt is on the ground and the corners
are cut off steeply — a 64-degree climb over three units, not a long shallow ramp.
What makes the ends read as raised is not the outline: it is the idler and the
sprocket being visible, small and off the ground INSIDE the loop.
3. THE BELT WRAPS. It is a loop, so it passes in front of the end wheels; they are not
wheels standing beside a strip. This is the single thing three passes got wrong.
4. IT IS LOW. The hull roof is 1.5 m on a 7.0 m hull — the famous 2.2 m is the TURRET
roof, and building to it makes a hull half again too tall.
5. THE GLACIS IS ENORMOUS AND VERY SHALLOW: 17 degrees off horizontal over a third of
the length. A steep front plate is the fastest way to make a Soviet tank look
Western.
6. THE FENDER IS THE WIDEST THING ON THE VEHICLE and it runs the entire length, past
the idler, ending in a hanging mud flap across the nose.
SCALE: 57 long, 28.5 wide, 13 tall, against the Mangal's 76 x 39 x 33. The two share a
pack and therefore a world scale, and a T-80 has to read as much the lower of the pair.
name: T80

t80.tga._: Soviet dark olive — greener and darker than the Mangal's drab. `ao` and `lip` are
t80.tga.__: the two fields that do the work: dark occlusion in every recess and a bright lip
t80.tga.___: on every top edge is the whole difference between a retail 256 vehicle sheet and
t80.tga.____: a flat one, and it is not a matter of colour or of frequency.
t80.tga._blobs: hatches 0. The panel generator places its round access hatches anywhere in a region, and on an atlas that meant three dark rings scattered across the GLACIS and the nose plate — the two surfaces on a tank that are unbroken armour. The deck gets its own region below and carries the grilles instead.

t80_wheel.tga._: Six road wheels between the belt's two runs, on their own tiling sheet because the
t80_wheel.tga.__: plate leaves the atlas: cube projection puts a thin offset plate's faces so far
t80_wheel.tga.___: apart in UV that a packed region sized to hold them all leaves the face that
t80_wheel.tga.____: matters sampling an empty band of itself. Both halves of opting out must agree —
t80_wheel.tga._____: `noAtlas` leaves the PACK and the TEXTURE, and leaving one behind is what once
t80_wheel.tga.______: rendered the Mangal's wheels as blocks.
t80_wheel.tga._______: runDepth is small because the belt above and below is real geometry here, not
t80_wheel.tga.________: paint, but not zero: the reference has the wheel row sitting between two shadowed strips, and at 0.05 the plate read as one flat band. wheelRadius 0.42 of the 7-unit tile gives a 5.9 wheel in a 5.6 opening, so the belt clips it top and bottom — the wheel is BEHIND the track, not inside it.

_: THE BELT, and the one sheet that cannot be a region of the atlas. W3DTankDraw animates
a track by adding to the mesh's U offset, so UVs confined to a packed rectangle would
scroll straight out of it and into whatever part owns the rectangle next door. Retail
splits at exactly this line — NVGattTank.tga for the body, NVTreads.tga for the belts.
NO PAINTED ROAD WHEELS (`wheels: 0`). A scrolling sheet carries only what genuinely
travels on a real track, which is the links. Here the wheels are geometry anyway.
COARSE ON PURPOSE. uvScale 16 over a 49-long return run repeats about three times, and
a pitch of 32 on a 128 sheet gives four links per repeat — twelve links of roughly four
world units each. A real T-80 has forty-odd, and forty-odd read as a stationary hatch
the moment they move. A moving texture must be legible at the speed it moves.
Darker than the hull but no longer MUCH darker. It was cut to 46 while the road wheels
were still geometry standing in front of it and the belt had to recede behind them.
With the wheels painted on a plate INSIDE the loop, the belt is the thing in front,
and at that tone its end wraps rendered as solid black fins rather than as track.
_edge: THE RIM SHADING IS ON, because under `uvMode: belt` V finally means something: the
sheet's height is the belt's WIDTH on every face, so the painter's two shaded bands
land on the belt's actual edges instead of wherever the projection happened to put
them. Under cube projection they were a hazard — a loop's runs are thin bars, so the
ground run sampled rows 0-5 of 128, entirely inside one band, while the return run
sampled rows 50-56 and got none of it. One track, one sheet, two materials.
The `edgeShadow` knob stays in the tool for any tread that is still projected.

t80_deck.tga._: THE ENGINE DECK, and it is the only place on a tank where a grille belongs. The
t80_deck.tga.__: T-80's rear deck is almost entirely louvres and radiator mesh, which is why the
t80_deck.tga.___: hull's own region now carries hatches 0 and this one carries six grilles: put them
t80_deck.tga.____: on the sheet's base spec and they land on the glacis instead.

t80_house.tga._: The team-colour plate, painted NEARLY WHITE deliberately. Recolour_Vertex_Material
t80_house.tga.__: SETS the vertex material's ambient and diffuse to the player's colour — the engine's
t80_house.tga.___: own comment says it ignores whatever was there and assumes 1.0 — and the texture
t80_house.tga.____: still modulates on top. So the pixel is texture x teamColour: a pale plate reads as
t80_house.tga._____: the team's actual colour and an olive one reads as muddy olive for everyone alike.

_: THE LEFT BELT. Two separately authored parts rather than one mirrored one, and the
NAME is the whole reason: W3DTankDraw finds a track by _strnicmp(meshName, "TREADS",
6) and reads the SEVENTH character for the side, scrolling L forward and R backward.
A mirrored mesh has one name and can therefore only be one side.
THE CONTACT PATCH IS ALMOST THE WHOLE TRACK. `size` is the GROUND RUN — 45 — and the
taper stretches the top out to 45 x 1.15 = 51.8, the return run. That is 3.4 units of
run against 7 of rise at each end: a 64-degree climb over a very short distance, with
87% of the belt's length on the ground.
Measured off a proper side-on photograph, and it reversed what three passes had built.
The earlier belt ran 33 on the ground against 49 on top — a 41-degree climb eating a
third of the track's length — which is a shape that reads as a bulldozer. A tank track
is very nearly a RECTANGLE with its corners cut off steeply; what makes the ends read
as raised is not the outline, it is the idler and the sprocket being visible and off
the ground inside it.
The taper is [1.485, 1.0] — LENGTH ONLY. A single factor scales both other axes and
would splay the belt outward as it rose, turning the track into a funnel.
AND IT IS HOLLOW. A solid trapezoid is a slab with a track painted on it, and the
giveaway is at the ENDS: the belt has to go AROUND the idler and the sprocket, and a
solid box cannot, so those two wheels ended up standing beside the belt with its flat
face behind them — the one thing a real track never does. Cutting the middle out
leaves the four bars that a track actually is: a ground run, a return run and a wrap
at each end. The road wheels then show THROUGH the opening rather than in front of it,
which is also why they moved inboard.
THE CUTTER TAPERS TOO, so the loop is a UNIFORM 0.7 thick the whole way round. A
rectangular hole in a trapezoid is not one: it leaves the runs 0.7 thick and the two
wraps 3.2, which is wrong as a track — a real belt does not fatten where it turns —
and it wrecks the arc-length unwrap, because depth-into-the-ring stops meaning
anything once the ring is four times thicker at one end. Texel density measured a
14.7x spread across the part; the correct cutter brings it to 1.0.
The numbers are the outer trapezoid offset inward by 0.7 PERPENDICULAR to each edge:
0.7 of z top and bottom, and 0.7/sin(64.3 deg) = 0.777 of x at the sloped ends, which
is why the inner run lengths are 44.12 and 49.52 rather than 43.6 and 50.35.
The opening is 5.2 of the belt's 7, leaving bars 0.9 thick. At 4.6 with a fat bevel
the bars closed over the wheels until each one read as a rounded SQUARE — the loop
has to be an opening the running gear shows through, not a slot it peers out of.
parts.name: TREADSL

parts._: The right belt. Authored rather than mirrored, for the naming reason above.
parts.name: TREADSR

_: THE RUNNING GEAR, PAINTED — and this reverses a decision three passes defended, on
measurement rather than taste. All 8,889 shipped models were scanned: 164 TREADS
sub-objects across 56 tanks, and exactly THREE of those 56 carry a wheel, roller,
sprocket or idler sub-object at all. Retail paints the road wheels on the static
CHASSIS and slides a thin belt over it. The modelled version cost 512 triangles — 53%
of the model, on a tank whose retail median is 327 WITH a turret and a gun.
IT MUST BE STATIC, and that is forced rather than stylistic. W3DTankDraw animates a
belt by sliding its whole sheet along U, so a road wheel painted on the belt travels
down the hull with the links. Wheels and track are one texture only while nothing
moves. Static plate, moving loop around it.
INSIDE the loop (y 11.6..12.4 against the belt's 8.2..12.6), so the belt still wraps in
front of it at both ends — which is the whole reason the belt became a loop and the
thing that was actually being complained about.
The UV numbers are not free choices, and they are what sets the plate's SIZE rather
than the other way round. `uvScale` 7.7 with the plate spanning z 0..7.7 lands V on
exactly 0..1 — the whole sheet once, no offset, no wrap — and U then runs 46.2/7.7 = 6
repeats, which at one wheel per tile is the six road wheels. Counts in a painter are
PER TILE, and `phase: 0` keeps them off the tile seams.
IT MUST REACH THE ENDS OF THE OPENING. At 42 long it stopped about two units short of
each wrap, and those two units were a view straight into the loop's unlit interior —
a black wedge at each corner of the vehicle, which is what reads as the tread sticking
out beyond the fender rather than tucking under it. 46.2 fills it. The plate then
stands 0.7 taller than the belt, which is free: the fender covers it.
parts.name: RUNGEAR

parts._: The lower hull: a plain box between and above the tracks, vertical-sided because a
parts.__: T-80's upper hull sides are vertical. Deck at z = 15.2, sponson floor at 6.8 — just
parts.___: above the return run, so no daylight opens between hull and track.
parts.name: HULL

_: THE GLACIS, and it is the largest single surface on the vehicle. A wedge rotated 90
degrees about z, which puts its narrow top strip at the REAR — so the plate descends
from the deck forward and down to the nose, which is the direction a tank's front
plate slopes and the opposite of what an unrotated wedge does.
22 DEGREES OFF HORIZONTAL, over 21 units of the hull's 58 — the slope alone is a
quarter of the whole vehicle. Reference photographs are unanimous and unintuitive
about this: the plate is nearly flat and enormously long, and the first instinct is a
short steep front, which is a Chieftain and not a T-80. The first pass here ran the
glacis over 16 units, of which only 11 were actually sloped, and it read as a chamfer
on the corner of a box.
It only spans z 11.5 to 17.0. The rest of the front is the NOSE below it, and the two
must span the SAME x range: the first pass had the glacis start at 13 and the nose at
17, which left a four-unit hole straight through the front of the tank at z 7..11.5.
It rendered as a small black notch under the glacis and nothing structural caught it.
parts.name: GLACIS

_: THE LOWER FRONT PLATE — everything under the glacis, spanning exactly the same x range
(8 to 29), because the two not spanning the same range is what left a four-unit hole
straight through the front of the tank on the first pass.
A WEDGE, NOT A BOX, and the rotation is the whole trick. On a Soviet tank the glacis
and the lower plate meet at a horizontal EDGE about a metre up, and the hull recedes
underneath it — the front is a shallow V on its side, not a wall. A box gives a blunt
vertical face at the nose and it is the difference between a tank and a skip.
rot [180, 0, -90] composes two flips to get there: the z-rotation puts the wedge's
narrow strip at the REAR and the x-rotation turns it upside down, so the part is full
length along its TOP and recedes to a rear strip along its BOTTOM. Unrotated, and with
either flip alone, the wedge comes out thick at the front and tapering to nothing at
the back — a plausible solid, and an overhang where the tank needs an undercut.
IT IS SHORT, AND THAT IS WHY BELLY EXISTS. A wedge's recession is fixed at 65% of its
length, so one wedge spanning the whole 21 units under the glacis cut 13.6 of undercut
into a hull 4.4 tall — the entire front of the tank became a cave, and with the mud
flap hanging in front of it the nose read as an open mouth. Over 8 units the same
wedge gives 5.2 of recession at 40 degrees, which is the shape the reference has, and
a plain box fills the flat part behind it for twelve triangles. Six units and 48
degrees is where it settled: the recess has to be short enough for the mud flap to
COVER, or the tank has a dark triangular cavity where its nose should be.
parts.name: NOSE

parts._: The flat belly under the glacis, between the hull's front face and the nose wedge.
parts.__: A plain box: nothing here is ever seen from above and only its flanks are seen at
parts.___: all, so it is twelve triangles that exist to stop the front being hollow.
parts.name: BELLY

_: THE FRONT MUD FLAP — the hanging plate under the nose, and one of the two or three
details that say 'Soviet' from a hundred metres.
IT HANGS BACK UNDER THE GLACIS, not off the leading edge. At x 25 against the nose tip
at 29 the front plate overhangs it, which is where it is actually bolted: off the front
of the FENDER, in front of the idler. Placed at the tip it stopped reading as a flap
under the tank and became the front of the tank.
IT SPANS EXACTLY BETWEEN THE TRACKS — 16.6 wide, meeting the belts' inner faces at
y = +-8.3. At 26 it ran the full width and the head-on view was one flat panel with the
running gear hidden behind it; at 15 it left a slot of unlit belly either side. A tank
presents TREADS at the front with a plate between them, and every reference frame is
unambiguous about it.
parts.name: MUDFLAP

parts._: The rear plate, standing a little proud of the hull so the back of the vehicle has
parts.__: an edge rather than being the end of a box.
parts.name: REARPLATE

_: THE FENDER, and it is doing two jobs at once because both are the same box. Its top
face is the shelf that runs the length of the tank and its outer face is the skirt lip
hanging over the belt — modelling those separately costs forty triangles to say what
one part already says.
It is THE WIDEST THING ON THE VEHICLE, out to y = 15.5 against the wheels' 14.6 and
the hull's 13. A tank whose hull is its widest point looks like a crate on tracks; the
overhang is what makes the running gear read as tucked underneath something.
It runs the full 55 and past the idler, which is where the mud flap hangs off it.
ITS UNDERSIDE OVERLAPS THE BELT rather than clearing it: 6.6 against the track's top
at 7.0. At 7.2 there was a 0.2 gap and the belt's top edge showed as a bright line the
length of the vehicle — a tread has to disappear UNDER the fender, not stop short of it.
parts.name: FENDER

parts._: STOWAGE ALONG THE FENDER — a long low box the length of the hull, which is what the
parts.__: reference has and what breaks up the single blankest surface on the model. The flank
parts.___: above the fender line is unbroken olive from the rear plate to the glacis, and no
parts.____: amount of texture fixes a wall; this puts a real shadow line halfway up it for
parts.name: STOWAGE

parts._: THE ENGINE DECK PANEL. Twelve triangles for the single flattest, emptiest surface
parts.__: on the model — the rear deck ran unbroken from the hatch line to the rear plate and
parts.___: read as a lid. Raised 0.55 proud so it casts its own line into the AO bake, and its
parts.____: region is the one carrying the grilles.
parts.name: DECKGRILLE

parts._: THE TEAM-COLOUR PLATE — the cheapest part on the model and the one that says whose
parts.__: tank it is. The engine finds it by mesh NAME, _strnicmp(meshName, "HOUSECOLOR", 10),
parts.___: and recolours the whole submesh's vertex material. A material is per-mesh, so this
parts.____: has to be its own part: a painted stripe on the hull could never be recoloured.
parts._____: On the hull's flat vertical flank, standing 0.7 proud — a flat plate belongs on a
parts.______: flat face, and chasing a sloped one is what moved the Mangal's three times.
parts.name: HOUSECOLOR01

_bones: Pivots with no geometry — how a model tells the engine something it cannot see.
computeTrackSpacing measures the distance between TREADFX01 and TREADFX02 and adds one
belt width to it to size the mud ribbon. Missing, it falls back to a constant sized for
nothing in particular. Placed at the belt CENTRELINES (y = +-11.6) at the rear of the
contact patch, so the two marks land under the two tracks and not beside them.
03 and 04 are the front pair. Nothing reads them — the engine takes 01 and 02 only — but
retail carries all four and a pivot costs 60 bytes.
_extra: A SHEET NO MESH NAMES. The mud the tracks leave is laid on the TERRAIN, not on the tank,
so nothing inside the .w3d points at it and the orphan check cannot find it — which is why
`extraTextures` exists as its own block rather than being inferred.
IT LIVES ON THE T-80 BECAUSE THE T-80 IS THE BASE TANK. The Mangal is derived from this
recipe and both units' compiled INI names track_rf.tga, but only one recipe needs to write
it. It used to live on the Mangal; deriving the Mangal FROM this file silently dropped it,
the pack kept declaring build/models/track_rf.tga in zh.art, the compiler kept emitting
TrackMarks = track_rf.tga, and nothing wrote the file — two tanks laying no mud, with no
error anywhere. e2e's zero-borrow gate caught it by demanding every declared file exist.

track_rf.tga._: 32-bit: the terrain-track shader is _PresetAlphaShader and the ALPHA channel IS the
track_rf.tga.__: mark. U runs across the ribbon and V alternates every other quad, so the sheet has
track_rf.tga.___: to be V-symmetric or the mark flickers as the strip is laid.
